questions.q: Under the Law and Equity Act s.59, which contract does NOT need writing to be enforceable?
choices: A contract to buy a strata lot
A 2-year lease of a retail unit
A 5-year lease of a warehouse
An option to purchase farmland
questions.explain: s.59 doesn't apply to leases (or agreements to lease) of 3 years or less.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · The requirement of writing

questions.q: Only the buyer signed a written note agreeing to buy a lot. Who can enforce it?
choices: Either party, against the other
The seller, against the buyer
The buyer, against the seller
Neither party, it's void
questions.explain: Writing binds the signer (the party to be charged). The seller can enforce against the buyer, not the reverse (absent conduct or reliance).
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · The requirement of writing

questions.q: Apart from signed writing, which can make an oral land contract enforceable under s.59?
choices: The licensee's own file notes on it
Accepting a deposit or part payment
A witness who overheard the deal
Registering a caveat on title later
questions.explain: Conduct (paying or accepting a deposit or part of the price) and reliance (changing position) are the other two routes.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · The requirement of writing

questions.q: In Pepper's Produce v. Medallion Realty, why was the licensee liable?
choices: They failed to deposit the buyer's cheque
They advised removing a subject on a verbal lease promise
They listed the grocery store without the owner's consent
They misstated the store's annual revenue
questions.explain: A lease over 3 years needs writing; the licensee should have known not to rely on the landlord's verbal yes.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · The requirement of writing

questions.q: A seller's signature arrives on a contract by email. Can you sign as witness?
choices: Yes, if you recognize the signature
No, a witness must actually see them sign
Yes, if the seller confirms it by phone
Only if your managing broker agrees to it
questions.explain: A witness must be 19+ and actually see the person sign. A licensee who witnessed remotely was disciplined.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · The requirement of writing

questions.q: In Brian Fisher Realty v. Emerald Park Lodge, why was no commission payable on a full-price cash offer?
choices: The licensee wasn't licensed at the time
It didn't match the listing's financing terms
The seller had already sold privately
The offer arrived after the listing expired
questions.explain: The listing asked for $30,000 down with vendor financing. An all-cash offer didn't strictly comply.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · Listing contracts

questions.q: Who are the parties to a listing contract?
choices: The buyer and the seller
The seller and the brokerage
The seller and the licensee personally
The brokerage and the buyer
questions.explain: The listing is between the seller and the brokerage. The buyer isn't a party and can't rely on its terms.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · Listing contracts

questions.q: In Bouskill v. Campea, a lot listed as 172 feet deep "more or less" was really 161 feet. Result?
choices: The buyer got a price reduction
The contract was unenforceable
"More or less" covered the gap
The seller had to buy more land
questions.explain: An 11-foot shortfall was too big for "more or less" to cover. Measure, or say how you know.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · Get the facts right at listing time

questions.q: A contract says the buyer will assume a mortgage of "approx. $20,000". Whose figure should you rely on?
choices: The seller's recollection
The lender's confirmation
The previous listing's figure
The buyer's estimate
questions.explain: Confirm the balance, rate, term, penalty and assumability with the lender. "The seller told me" is no defence.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · Get the facts right at listing time

questions.q: In Jung v. Ip, what share of the buyers' damages fell on the listing licensee?
choices: Nothing at all
All of it
questions.explain: A 15-minute inspection and "move-in condition" in a known termite area: the licensee bore 20%, and the employer also had a duty to verify.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · Get the facts right at listing time

questions.q: Which case shows why a title search matters, where "clear title" was promised despite two registered easements?
choices: Bouskill v. Campea
Price v. Malais
Jung v. Ip
Lee v. Skalbania
questions.explain: The buyers walked away and the brokerage breached its duty to the seller.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · Get the facts right at listing time

questions.q: Which is most likely a criminal conspiracy under Competition Act s.45?
choices: Two agents agreeing the split on one sale
Brokerages agreeing a minimum commission rate
A brokerage choosing its own commission rate
A board publishing average sale prices
questions.explain: Fixing commission rates or splits among competitors is a classic s.45 conspiracy. Agreeing a split on a particular sale is fine.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · Criminal provisions

questions.q: What's the maximum prison term for a s.45 conspiracy?
choices: 2 years
14 years
5 years
1 year
questions.explain: Up to 14 years and/or a fine at the court's discretion.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · Criminal provisions

questions.q: What must the Crown prove for a s.45 conspiracy conviction?
choices: That competition was actually harmed
An agreement, which may be implied
That the agreement was carried out
That consumers paid higher prices
questions.explain: No proof of harm or performance is needed, and an agreement can be inferred from circumstances.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · Criminal provisions

questions.q: Which statement about s.52 (misleading advertising) is correct?
choices: Puffery like "best view in town" is an offence
Nobody needs to have actually been misled
It only applies to printed advertising
Only a literal falsehood can be misleading
questions.explain: Courts consider literal meaning and general impression; actual deception isn't required. Puffery isn't material.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · Criminal provisions

questions.q: Why do most misleading-advertising cases go under s.74.01 rather than s.52?
choices: It carries longer prison terms
It doesn't require proof of intent
It only applies to licensees
It's heard by the criminal courts
questions.explain: s.74.01 is civil and needs no intent; first-time AMPs reach $750,000 for individuals and $10 million for corporations.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · Civil provisions (heard by the Competition Tribunal)

questions.q: Under s.74.05, who is NOT exempt from the ban on selling above the advertised price?
choices: A licensee selling a resale home for an owner
A licensee selling units for a developer
A licensee selling a commercial building for an owner
A licensee leasing an office for an owner
questions.explain: Owners' licensees are exempt (getting the best price is the job). Developers' licensees aren't.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · Civil provisions (heard by the Competition Tribunal)

questions.q: A board refuses to list properties whose commission is "too low". Which provision is most relevant?
choices: s.52 misleading advertising
s.76 price maintenance
s.74.05 sale above advertised price
s.90.1 lease exclusivity
questions.explain: Punishing someone for low pricing is price maintenance.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · Civil provisions (heard by the Competition Tribunal)

questions.q: Under CPS clause 16, when does risk of loss pass to the buyer?
choices: When the contract is accepted by both
At 12:01 a.m. on the Completion Date
When all subjects have been removed
On the Possession Date in the contract
questions.explain: The property stays at the seller's risk until 12:01 a.m. on the Completion Date, reversing the equitable default.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · The contract of purchase and sale

questions.q: The house burns down between subject removal and completion. Is the contract frustrated?
choices: Yes, fire always frustrates a sale contract
No, the CPS provides for it (seller's risk)
Yes, unless the buyer had arranged insurance
No, the buyer must complete it as is
questions.explain: Because the contract allocates the risk, frustration doesn't apply. The property is at the seller's risk.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · The contract of purchase and sale

questions.q: Two buyers don't say how they'll hold title. What do BC courts presume?
choices: Joint tenancy
Tenancy in common
Ownership by the first-named buyer
A trust for both buyers
questions.explain: Tenancy in common is presumed. Explain the options, but don't advise which to pick.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · The three P's: parties, property, price

questions.q: Under the federal ban, what fine can a licensee face for helping a non-Canadian buy residential property?
choices: Up to $1,000
questions.explain: Anyone who helps break the ban faces up to $10,000, plus BCFSA discipline.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · The three P's: parties, property, price

questions.q: Which purchase is NOT caught by the non-Canadian ban?
choices: A condo in a census metropolitan area
Vacant residentially zoned land
A townhouse in a census agglomeration
A detached home in Metro Vancouver
questions.explain: Vacant land isn't "residential property" under the Act, and buying for development is exempt.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · The three P's: parties, property, price

questions.q: How should you describe part of a parcel that hasn't yet been subdivided?
choices: By civic address alone
By metes and bounds with a sketch
By the whole parcel's PID
By the seller's verbal description
questions.explain: Use metes and bounds with landmarks and an attached sketch, or risk the contract being void for uncertainty.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · The three P's: parties, property, price

questions.q: In Block Bros. v. Occidental Hotel, what killed the contract?
choices: The buyer's deposit cheque bounced
"And/or" financing wording was uncertain
The buyer was under 19 at signing
The listing had already expired by then
questions.explain: The two financing methods are completely different. No contract, so no commission.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · The three P's: parties, property, price

questions.q: A buyer's offer says the balance is payable by agreement for sale "under the usual terms". What happened in Buyers v. Begg?
choices: The court supplied standard terms
Too vague; the buyer got the deposit back
The seller kept the deposit
The court ordered specific performance
questions.explain: There are no "usual" terms, so there was no enforceable contract and the deposit was returned.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · The three P's: parties, property, price

questions.q: An offer is accepted on Thursday, July 6. When does the HBRP end?
choices: End of Sunday, July 9
End of Tuesday, July 11
End of Monday, July 10
End of Wednesday, July 12
questions.explain: The period starts the next business day (Friday) and skips Saturday and Sunday: Friday, Monday, Tuesday.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · The Home Buyer Rescission Period (HBRP)

questions.q: A buyer rescinds a $1,200,000 purchase under the HBRP. What do they owe the seller?
choices: Nothing
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · The Home Buyer Rescission Period (HBRP)

questions.q: Which purchase is NOT covered by the HBRP?
choices: A residential strata lot
A home bought at auction
A semi-detached house
A manufactured home on owned land
questions.explain: Auction, court-ordered, leasehold and REDMA development unit sales are excluded.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · The Home Buyer Rescission Period (HBRP)

questions.q: A rescission notice is sent by registered mail. When is it deemed delivered?
choices: When the seller signs for it
When it's sent
Three days after mailing
When the seller's agent opens it
questions.explain: Registered mail: when sent. Fax or email with read receipt requested: when transmitted.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · The Home Buyer Rescission Period (HBRP)

questions.q: Your brokerage holds the deposit and the buyer validly rescinds under the HBRP. What do you do?
choices: Wait for both parties to sign a release
Pay the seller 0.25% and return the rest
Pay the whole deposit into court
Hold it until the completion date passes
questions.explain: No release is needed: pay the 0.25% to the seller and promptly return the balance to the buyer.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · The Home Buyer Rescission Period (HBRP)

questions.q: How long must a brokerage keep HBRP rescission notices?
choices: 1 year
7 years
3 years
5 years
questions.explain: They're trading records: kept 7 years and reported in the annual activity report.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · The Home Buyer Rescission Period (HBRP)

questions.q: What is the consideration in a contract of purchase and sale?
choices: The deposit
The exchange of promises
The commission
The title transfer fee
questions.explain: The promises to transfer title and to pay are the consideration. A contract can be binding before any deposit is paid.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · Terms, conditions and the deposit

questions.q: Unless agreed otherwise, when must the deposit be paid under CPS clause 2?
choices: On completion
Within 24 hours of acceptance
Within 3 business days
Within 7 days of acceptance
questions.explain: Within 24 hours of acceptance. Failing to pay lets the seller terminate.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · Terms, conditions and the deposit

questions.q: A deal collapses. The buyer demands their deposit back; the seller says nothing. What can the brokerage do?
choices: Return it to the buyer, since they paid it
Only release it with all parties' signed release
Give it all to the seller as liquidated damages
Split it equally between buyer and seller
questions.explain: As stakeholder (RESA s.28), release requires all parties' agreement, HBRP rescission, or payment into court.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · The brokerage as stakeholder (RESA s.28)

questions.q: The buyer says "I've stopped payment on the deposit cheque, give it back." What do you do?
choices: Return the cheque to the buyer
Deposit it and tell the seller's side
Shred it and record the event
Hold it until the buyer calms down
questions.explain: Stakeholder rules apply even to an undeposited cheque. Deposit it and notify the seller's side immediately.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · The brokerage as stakeholder (RESA s.28)

questions.q: In Lee v. Skalbania, could the seller keep the $50,000 deposit after reselling for $31,000 more?
choices: No, the profit offset the loss
Yes, the deposit was reasonable
No, deposits are always refunded
Only half of it
questions.explain: 5–10% deposits are reasonable; relief under LEA s.24 needs an unreasonable deposit and unconscionability.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · The brokerage as stakeholder (RESA s.28)

questions.q: By default, who gets interest earned on deposits held in a brokerage trust account?
choices: The buyer who paid the deposit
The Real Estate Foundation
The seller receiving the deposit
The brokerage holding the funds
questions.explain: Unless the parties agree otherwise (which needs a separate trust account), interest goes to the Real Estate Foundation.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · The brokerage as stakeholder (RESA s.28)

questions.q: What does the doctrine of merger mean for a buyer after completion?
choices: They can sue on any promise in the CPS
Most contract promises can't be sued on
They get a 2-year warranty period
They can reopen the price within 30 days
questions.explain: The contract merges into the transfer; buyers must check things before completing. CPS clause 18 preserves written warranties.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · Warranties and the doctrine of merger

questions.q: Which is NOT an exception to the doctrine of merger?
choices: Fraud
A licensee's verbal assurance
A collateral warranty meant to survive
A statutory warranty
questions.explain: Verbal assurances aren't an exception. Put relied-on assurances into the CPS as express warranties.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · Warranties and the doctrine of merger

questions.q: In Olszewski v. Trapman, why did the buyer get the $100,000 deposit back?
choices: The seller had committed fraud
They refused to complete before closing
The lot turned out larger than described
The licensee was not licensed at the time
questions.explain: A 1.15-acre lot sold as approx. 1.5 acres: innocent misrepresentation can support rescission while the contract is still executory.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · Warranties and the doctrine of merger

questions.q: When buying a strata lot from the owner developer, what holdback is required by law?
choices: 10% of the price
7% of the gross price
5% of the deposit
None
questions.explain: Strata Property Act s.88 and Regulation s.5.2 require a 7% holdback, released at the earlier of the last lien-filing date or 55 days.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · Builders liens and Norfolk & Aikens

questions.q: What does the Norfolk & Aikens procedure allow?
choices: Builders to file liens after 55 days
Registration on lawyers' undertakings
Buyers to skip the holdback
Sellers to keep the deposit
questions.explain: CPS clauses 13–14 let transfers and mortgages register on lawyers' and notaries' undertakings, so both sides can use the proceeds.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · Builders liens and Norfolk & Aikens

questions.q: Under CPS clause 3, how must a subject be removed?
choices: Verbally, by either of the parties
By written notice from the benefiting party
Automatically when the subject date arrives
By the licensees acting on either side
questions.explain: Written notice, on or before the date. Otherwise the contract terminates.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · Removing subjects

questions.q: Under LEA s.54, which is NOT required to waive a true condition precedent?
choices: It benefits only the waiving party
The other party's written consent
The contract can be performed without it
Waiver before the deadline
questions.explain: s.54 lets the sole beneficiary waive without the other side's consent.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · Removing subjects

questions.q: "Subject to approval by the buyer company's president" is best described as what?
choices: Wholly objective
Wholly subjective
Partly objective
A covenant
questions.explain: Pure whim and fancy: probably no binding contract yet, just a revocable offer.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · Subjective vs objective subjects

questions.q: In Harris v. Wang, why were the buyers liable for $274,000?
choices: They forgot to pay the deposit on time
They stopped trying to satisfy their subjects
They removed subjects too early
They assigned the contract without consent
questions.explain: After learning of a natural death in the house, they simply stopped arranging financing and inspection: no good faith.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · Trying in good faith to satisfy a subject

questions.q: Per Gordon Nelson v. Cameron, what does "in their sole discretion" do to a financing subject?
choices: Makes the whole subject void
Lowers the standard to honest efforts
Raises the standard to best efforts
Converts the subject into a covenant
questions.explain: Without those words, Griffin v. Martens requires best efforts. The exact wording matters.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · Trying in good faith to satisfy a subject

questions.q: In Gulston v. Aldred, "the Seller shall remedy the contamination by May 29" was treated as what?
choices: A condition precedent
A covenant
A collateral warranty
A time clause
questions.explain: "Shall" made it an unconditional promise. The late certificate didn't let the buyer walk; only damages.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · Seven drafting best practices

questions.q: What does a time clause let a seller with a backup offer do?
choices: Cancel the first contract whenever it likes
Force the first buyer to remove subjects quickly
Raise the price payable by the first buyer
Accept both offers and pick one later
questions.explain: Written notice requires removal within a set time (typically 24–72 hours) or the contract ends.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · Seven drafting best practices

questions.q: What wording should you add when changing a completion date?
choices: "All prior dates are cancelled"
"Time remains of the essence"
"Subject to the buyer's approval"
"This replaces the original contract"
questions.explain: Clause 12 makes time of the essence; restate it: "All other terms and conditions remain the same and time remains of the essence."
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · Amending a contract

questions.q: Why avoid naming the buyer as "John Smith and/or nominee"?
choices: It doubles the property transfer tax owed
It may make the buyer's identity uncertain
It is expressly prohibited under RESA
It automatically triggers the buyer's HBRP
questions.explain: Dunbar v. Dayson Holdings: it can make the contract uncertain.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · Assigning a contract of purchase and sale

questions.q: Which developments does CSAIR reporting apply to?
choices: Any commercial strata development in BC
Residential strata developments of 5+ lots
All new single-family home subdivisions
Bare land strata developments of 10+ lots
questions.explain: Residential strata developments of 5 or more lots; developers collect and report the assignment data.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · CSAIR (Condo and Strata Assignment Integrity Register)

questions.q: What's your BATNA?
choices: The first offer you put on the table
Your best alternative if no deal is made
The highest target you aspire to reach
The other side's walk-away bottom line
questions.explain: A strong BATNA gives you power and calm; your resistance point is your bottom line.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · Preparation (the single biggest improvement)

questions.q: A buyer insists on a June 17 completion. What's the integrative response?
choices: Hold firm on the opposite date
Ask why, to find the interest behind it
Split the difference on the date
Threaten to walk away from the deal
questions.explain: The position may hide an interest (e.g. can't carry two mortgages) that other solutions could meet.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · Preparation (the single biggest improvement)

questions.q: The other side keeps saying "my partner won't approve that." What tactic is this?
choices: Anchoring
False authority
Eleventh-hour throw-in
Reciprocal concession
questions.explain: Confirm up front who decides, and treat any deal as tentative until they agree.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · Dirty tactics, and how to respond

questions.q: What's the coverage limit of the mandatory E&O Indemnity Plan?
questions.explain: $2,000,000. It excludes prior acts and property management.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · 1. Shift the risk

questions.q: Which statement about the Property Disclosure Statement is correct?
choices: BC law requires every seller to give one
Its answers are not a warranty
It replaces the licensee's s.59 duty entirely
It was created by BCFSA in 2018
questions.explain: BCREA created it in 1992. It's not legally required, and answers reflect only the seller's current knowledge.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · The Property Disclosure Statement (PDS)

questions.q: In Sewell v. Abadian (2025 BCCA), why did the buyer get its $300,000 deposit back?
choices: The seller never gave the buyer a PDS at all
A crossed-out PDS still implied no known issues
The licensee forgot to incorporate the PDS
The home turned out to be in a flood zone
questions.explain: The seller knew of an unpermitted addition. Read as a whole, the crossed-out form still misled. This prompted the PNDS.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · The Property Disclosure Statement (PDS)

questions.q: Why incorporate the PDS into the CPS?
choices: To avoid paying property transfer tax
So the buyer can sue on false answers
To extend the HBRP by 3 days
Because RESA requires it
questions.explain: The entire agreement clause otherwise blocks most claims on non-fraudulent PDS answers.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · The Property Disclosure Statement (PDS)

questions.q: Since when must BC home inspectors be licensed?
choices: January 1, 2023
March 31, 2009
June 2012
January 1, 1992
questions.explain: Since March 31, 2009, under the Business Practices and Consumer Protection Act. Check the licence before referring.
questions.ref: Lesson 8 · Environmental risk
